text:
"I don't have the energy to actually go to a temple. So I just sit here for a little while before leaving."
A virtual Buddhist temple created with artificial intelligence (AI) by a 26-year-old Korean job seeker has become an unexpected online hit, drawing more than 1 million visitors less than a week after its launch.
Called "Sansa," the digital space lets users control a child-monk avatar that can put its palms together in prayer or perform Buddhist bows. Visitors can also use their mouse to roll prayer beads or strike a moktak, a wooden percussion instrument used in Korean Buddhist rituals.
Sansa was launched on Oct. 26 by Park Jin-won, 26, who is looking for a job after graduating from university with a degree in English literature.
"There are days when I feel like it would be nice to go to a temple, but actually going requires you to make an effort," Park said.
That thought inspired the creation of an AI-powered Buddhist temple that people could enter through their phones.
Since the launch, Park has been sharing Sansa's visitor numbers and updates to the virtual temple on social media. A feature has also been introduced allowing users to support the project through an offering of rice, drawing on the traditional Buddhist practice of donating rice to temples.
More than 10,000 people visited Sansa on its first day, quickly putting its server under strain. Park increased its simultaneous user capacity from just 20 people to 10,000 and has since been working intensively to stabilize the service.
By Oct. 31, just five days after its launch, Sansa had recorded more than 900,000 cumulative visits. It subsequently passed the 1 million mark.
Users have also flooded Park with suggestions for new features, including a virtual version of "tapdori," the Buddhist practice of walking around a pagoda, and an option for a monk to strike users with a jukbi, a bamboo stick traditionally used in Zen meditation.
Sansa's viral success has already inspired a wave of similar virtual spaces.
Online-only Catholic churches and Protestant churches have appeared, along with less spiritual destinations where users can virtually board a plane and eat an in-flight meal, visit a sauna or hot spring, camp outdoors or even explore a coal mine.
The trend has drawn attention to how generative AI is allowing individuals to rapidly turn simple but imaginative ideas into interactive online experiences.
"All they did was take the act of visiting a temple, something people normally do offline, and move it online, but that captured people's interest," one social media user said. "It seems you don't have to create some grand service to attract people."
Another said, "We've entered an era where you can sit in your room and experience all kinds of healing through a single web browser."
This article from the Hankook Ilbo, the sister publication of The Korea Times, was translated by a generative AI system and edited by The Korea Times.
